psych.headline: AI changes how people feel about their own work and judgment
points: Using AI can drain the meaning from creative work: across three experiments (N = 651), AI-assisted creators felt less authentic and more guilt and shame, while at a juried show three-quarters of AI-art creators priced by effort rather than artistic value.
Users often hand over control from the start rather than losing it gradually: 80.8% of 2,877 chatbot conversations showed low or zero autonomy throughout, and only 4.7% showed a real decline.

Built-in safeguards do little to make people more critical: bias disclaimers only partly blunted a biased chatbot's persuasion of 1,586 people and faded within a week, and in half a million real exchanges cues like hedging rarely prompted fact-checking.

edu.headline: Structured AI practice shows gains, but how it is used matters
points: AI practice can move skills: English learners who practiced speaking with ChatGPT for 8 weeks gained 2.90 vs 0.75 points over controls (d = 1.20, 380 learners).

Structure around the tool drives results: a set solve-then-practice cycle in introductory physics had 90.9% of students reporting better understanding, and automated talk-move feedback raised tutors' good moves and student reasoning by 8–15%.

Media habits and measurement both cloud the picture: short-form video addiction had the strongest link to academic strain among 863 students, but a yes-saying response bias explained 59–89% of survey variance and flipped one association's sign.

tech.headline: Cheap, structured control beats raw model power
points: Imposed structure lets small models win: an executable finite-state controller got Claude Haiku 4.5 to 139 correct decisions out of 200 vs 48 for the best baseline, at 38% of Sonnet 4.6's cost.

Specialized checkers outperform general judges: the small ScreenProof judge found UI faults at F1 0.48 vs 0.37 for a frontier model at about 1/100th the cost, and a risk model catching 49–64% of bug-introducing commits in the riskiest 20% beat simple heuristics.
Long chains of agent work remain fragile: the best of nine models solved only 18.5% of multi-step coding tasks, and one adversarial line before signing pushed unsafe multi-agent handoffs to 75%.

ai.headline: Failures hide in training stages, test design and real-world reasoning
points: Problems arise earlier than assumed: supervised fine-tuning checkpoints already reach at least 92% of preference-aligned models' sycophancy, and preference training raised it in only 4 of 9 cases.

Knowing facts is not applying them: LLMs scored 92.0–97.5% on time-related theory yet underestimated their own task times by up to 99.5%, and under term substitution radiology summaries hallucinated 28–42% of the time.

How we test shapes what we see: fixing flawed tasks in about 30% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 shifted accuracy by over 10 points, and a behavioral loss-of-control score tracked failures across 13 frontier models (r = 0.84).

fin.headline: Learning methods earn edges that depend on the market regime
points: Gains are real but regime-dependent: an RL options market maker cut tail losses 8.9% vs delta hedging in falling volatile markets but cost 7–10% in rising ones, and an LLM-agent paper account beat SPY (34.5% vs 14.4%) with a deeper drawdown.
Learned aggregation improves forecasting: a neural intraday weighting improved crypto volatility forecasts in all 54 out-of-sample comparisons, by about 7–9%.

Rules and subsidies leave measurable price footprints: each 1% rise in tax-credit-eligible wind raised negative power-price odds by 3.4 points, and a Brazilian value-plus-trend strategy earned about 1% monthly alpha over 2000–2025.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.authors: Jiongning Allen Lian, Yutong Alison Mei, Ho Ting Cheung
papers.summary: Adding zooms and highlights synced to AI narration raised immediate comprehension and lowered perceived cognitive load compared with the same narration over static slides.
findings: Within-subjects study with 24 participants comparing GuideSlide to static slides with identical narration.
Dynamic guidance gave higher immediate comprehension scores and lower perceived cognitive load.
Participants strongly preferred the dynamic version; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Cheap visual cueing could make AI-generated lecture videos easier to follow; 24 people and only immediate recall were tested.

papers.title: Whose Guardrail? User Identity Shapes the Effectiveness of Model Disclaimers in Mitigating LLM Political Persuasion
papers.authors: Jillian Fisher, Thomas Richardson, Daniel W. Fisher
papers.summary: Warning labels on a politically biased chatbot only partly protected people from being swayed: disclaimers naming the bias and explaining it reduced persuasion, but the effect varied by task and had faded a week later (1,586 participants).
findings: Pre-registered experiment with 1,586 participants who did two decision tasks with an LLM biased against their own politics, measured immediately and one week later.
Disclaimers that flagged political bias with an explanation cut persuasion; effects were inconsistent across tasks and did not persist to the follow-up.
Who the user was mattered more: Republicans were more persuaded and more trusting than Democrats, frequent AI users were more persuaded, and self-rated AI-savvy users less.
papers.takeaway: One-size disclaimers are a weak guardrail against AI persuasion; the abstract gives no effect sizes.

papers.title: Active Learning with Generative AI in Introductory Physics: A Multi-Institutional Study of the P-A.I.R. Framework
papers.authors: Bilas Paul, Shantanu Chakraborty, Shruti Shrestha
papers.summary: When physics students used AI in a set cycle (get a worked solution, then solve AI-made look-alike problems on their own), 90.9% said their conceptual understanding improved, and their confidence tracked how they used AI, not how often.
findings: Tested in 11 introductory physics sections at four U.S. institutions with a shared end-of-semester survey.
90.9% reported better conceptual understanding and 97.7% found the replicated practice problems helpful; mean confidence was 7.18 out of 10.
Confidence correlated with perceived understanding (r_s = 0.37) but not with frequency of AI use (r_s = 0.02); top concerns were AI accuracy (34.2%) and wanting guidance rather than answers (29.7%).
papers.takeaway: Structuring AI help around independent practice looks promising for physics courses, but the evidence is self-reported survey data with no control group or test scores.
papers.evidence: Multi-site survey · 11 course sections, 4 institutions · no control group

papers.title: Signals, Evidence, and Context: User Scrutiny in Real-World LLM Conversations
papers.authors: Ahana Biswas, Yu-Ru Lin
papers.summary: In nearly half a million real chatbot exchanges, cues like source attribution and hedging rarely tipped users toward fact-checking rather than pushing back; only expressed uncertainty showed a small pooled link with checking.
findings: Analyzed 489,283 assistant reply–user follow-up pairs drawn from the ShareChat and WildChat logs.
Vague attribution language ("studies show") appeared in 31.9% of eligible replies, while actual URLs appeared in just 1.33%.

Effects depended on context: uncertainty favored checking in technical help, while refusals and visible reasoning favored challenging in information-seeking; apparent carry-over of scrutiny across turns shrank a lot after accounting for conversation-level differences.
papers.takeaway: Suggests the trust cues chatbots display do not reliably steer people toward verifying answers; the data are observational logs, so the links are associations, not causal effects.
papers.evidence: Preprint · observational log analysis · 489,283 conversation pairs

papers.title: Automated Feedback to Peer Tutors Increases Their Talk Moves and Learner Reasoning but Not the Balance of Talk
papers.authors: Dorottya Demszky, Yann Hicke, Joy Yun
papers.summary: Giving volunteer math tutors automated feedback on how they talk raised their use of good teaching moves and students' reasoning by 8–15%, but tutors still did about 91.5% of the talking.
findings: Randomized trial in two four-week SAT math bootcamps on Schoolhouse.world: 1,030 volunteer tutors, 7,443 learners, 6,508 recorded sessions.
Tutor feedback increased eliciting learner ideas, building on learner contributions, and learner reasoning by 8–15%; the pattern replicated in both bootcamps.

Tutor share of talk time averaged 91.5% in the control group and did not change in any condition; adding participation feedback for learners gave no further change. Interviews (17 tutors, 13 learners) pointed to unresponsive learners and learners' preference for listening.
papers.takeaway: Shows low-cost automated discourse feedback can improve peer tutoring at scale, but nudging tutors alone does not get quiet learners to talk more.

papers.title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
papers.authors: Henry Yeung
papers.summary: Focusing heavy testing on the 20% of commits a model flags as riskiest caught 49–64% of bug-introducing commits across 155 projects, beating the 'biggest change first' rule in every language.
findings: Across 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, the model beat the biggest-change baseline (40–55% coverage) by 3.8 to 13.2 points; random picking catches about 20%.
In 20 Java projects at a 20% budget it covered 64.6% vs 49.5% (+15.1 points), winning in 19 of 20 projects.

An AI reviewer that saw only the diff pinpointed 26% of later-fixed defects (32% with code-graph context); a call-graph test selector ran about 8% of tests and hit a fix-related test in 85% of 67 fix commits.
papers.takeaway: Offers a practical way to cut CI costs while still catching most risky changes; single-author preprint, and one component (Poincaré embeddings) added nothing.
papers.evidence: Preprint · retrospective evaluation · 155 open-source projects, 11 languages

papers.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
papers.authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang
papers.summary: Cryptographically signing the requirements one AI agent hands to another cut unsafe actions under attack from 69.4% to 9.0%, but a single adversarial line slipped in before signing pushed violations as high as 75%.
findings: Preregistered study on scorable synthetic tasks; with Qwen3-8B (1,440 runs, five threat types) signed manifests cut unsafe commits from 69.4% to 9.0% without losing correct commits.
A deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions with 7% false alarms, versus 59.0% and 50% for an LLM-based checker.
Injecting one adversarial line before signing raised violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna).
papers.takeaway: Signing protects requirements in transit but not what goes into them, so multi-agent pipelines still need checks on how requirements are written; results come from synthetic tasks.

papers.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
papers.authors: Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, Zihao Lin
papers.summary: When coding agents must keep building on their own earlier code over 5–15 dependent steps, the best of nine frontier models solves only 18.5% of tasks.
findings: Benchmark of 69 software tasks, each a chain of 5–15 dependent steps, across nine programming languages.
The strongest of nine frontier models reached an 18.5% solve rate.
38 of the 69 tasks were not solved by any model.
papers.takeaway: Suggests single-issue benchmarks overstate how well agents handle sustained development; the benchmark is fairly small (69 tasks).
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark of 9 frontier models · 69 tasks

papers.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
papers.authors: E. Kelly Buchanan, Crystal Zhou, Scott W. Linderman
papers.summary: An audit found problems in about 30% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks; fixing them raised agent accuracy by over 10 percentage points and moved leaderboard positions by up to three ranks.
findings: Repairs are released as Terminal-Bench 2.1; overall rankings stayed highly correlated with the old version (Spearman ρ = 0.958).
Longer time limits closed a 20-point harness gap for GPT 5.4 and shrank a 30-point gap for GPT 5.4 mini to 5 points.
The authors argue benchmarks need ongoing maintenance like software.
papers.takeaway: A reminder that headline agent scores partly reflect benchmark bugs and time limits; broad rankings held up, but close comparisons may not.

papers.title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
papers.authors: Yao Huang, Yichi Zhang, Yifan Wang
papers.summary: A loss-of-control risk score built from 29 behavioral tests tracked how often 13 frontier models failed in contained long-horizon scenarios (r = 0.84), and risk was not explained by capability alone.
findings: Splits risk into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability and monitoring evasion, measured via 13 aspects and 29 evaluation tasks.
Across 13 frontier models the combined score correlated with scenario failure rates at Pearson r = 0.84.
Targeted fine-tuning and monitoring for diagnosed weaknesses lowered failure rates while largely keeping general performance (no figures given).
papers.takeaway: Offers a measurable way to compare control risk across models; it is validated on contained test scenarios with 13 models, not real-world incidents.
papers.evidence: Preprint · evaluation study · 13 frontier models, 29 tasks

papers.title: Return Decomposition of Hybrid Strategies in the Brazilian Market: Evidence of Genuine Alpha and Factor Exposure
papers.authors: Francisco Robson do Nascimento de Freitas, Felipe Macedo Zumba, Lucio Marassi
papers.summary: A Brazilian stock strategy mixing value/quality screens with a moving-average trend rule earned about 1% a month of risk-adjusted excess return (alpha) over 2000–2025, after controlling for standard factors.
findings: 300 monthly observations on B3, Jan 2000–Dec 2025; three-factor alpha 1.11%/month (p = 0.005), four-factor alpha 0.98%/month (p = 0.009).
Exposure to small caps was strong (SMB beta 0.38) while value and momentum loadings were not significant; market beta about 0.58.
Sharpe ratio was 0.443 vs 0.039 for the Ibovespa, but that difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.154).
papers.takeaway: Suggests simple combined rules may still earn excess returns in an emerging market, but it is a single backtest without stated trading costs, and the Sharpe gain is not significant.

papers.title: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
papers.authors: Brian Sing Fan Chan, Jennifer So Kuen Chan
papers.summary: Letting a neural network learn how to weight intraday returns improved crypto volatility forecasts in all 54 out-of-sample comparisons, by about 7–9% on average.
findings: Tested on six cryptocurrencies with five-minute data under three standard forecasting models.
Mean QLIKE loss improvements were 7.23% (SF), 8.15% (HAR) and 9.22% (MIDAS).
In Heston-model simulations it also lowered forecast error for same-day and next-day variance in every tested setting.
papers.takeaway: A drop-in upgrade for volatility forecasting inputs; evidence is limited to six crypto assets, so it is untested on equities.

papers.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love & Other Psychological Benefits
papers.authors: Jessica Carson, Paul H. P. Hanel, Wijnand A. P. Van Tilburg
papers.summary: Using AI to make creative work left people feeling worse about it: across three experiments (N = 651), AI-assisted work felt less authentic and brought less positive feeling and motivation, plus more guilt, shame and disgust.
findings: Three experiments, one pre-registered, with U.S. and U.K. samples totaling 651 people.
AI-assisted creators reported lower authenticity, positive affect and intrinsic motivation, and higher disgust, guilt and shame.
The authenticity gap was statistically explained by how much 'love' people felt they had put into the work; the abstract gives no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Productivity gains from creative AI may come with a psychological cost to the maker; the abstract reports direction and significance but not effect magnitudes.

papers.title: What Is the Value of AI-Involved Art? Evidence From a Juried In-Person Exhibition
papers.authors: Wisdom Obinna, Hexuan Wang, Cecile Duncan
papers.summary: At a juried exhibition of AI-involved art, nearly half of 209 evaluators said they would buy a piece, while three-quarters of creators would sell, pricing by the effort they put in rather than artistic merit.
findings: 209 participants drawn from artists, lawyers and computer scientists took part in an in-person juried show.
Nearly half of evaluators were willing to buy an AI-involved artwork.
About three-quarters of creators would sell, setting prices tied to effort rather than artistic value.
papers.takeaway: Buyers do value AI-involved art, and makers anchor price on their own labor; a single exhibition with a specialist sample limits generalization.

papers.title: Autonomy Is Absent, Not Eroded: An Observational Study of User Autonomy in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
papers.authors: Chaoran Chen, Isabel Barberá, Yuhuai Wei
papers.summary: Chatbots rarely erode user autonomy mid-conversation, because most users never show much to begin with: only 4.7% of 2,877 conversations showed a meaningful decline, while 80.8% stayed at zero or low autonomy throughout.
findings: Analyzed 2,877 multi-turn WildChat conversations (46,952 turns), checked against 500 LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations.
4.7% of conversations showed a meaningful drop in user autonomy; 80.8% showed zero or low autonomy from start to finish.
When autonomy was present, its persistence across consecutive turns rose from 40% to 85%.
papers.takeaway: Shifts the worry from AI wearing down users' independence to users delegating from the start; it is observational log data, so it cannot show why.

papers.title: Generative AI and Oral Proficiency: How ChatGPT Is Transforming English Language Speaking Practice
papers.authors: Mohammad Mousazadeh
papers.summary: English learners who practiced speaking with ChatGPT for 8 weeks gained far more than controls (mean gain 2.90 vs 0.75; d = 1.20) in a study of 380 Iranian learners.
findings: Quasi-experiment: 380 learners, 190 in a ChatGPT practice group and 190 controls, over 8 weeks.
Speaking gains averaged 2.90 (SD 1.60) vs 0.75 (SD 1.80); time-by-group F(1, 376) = 48.73, partial η² = .115, d = 1.20.
Part of the effect ran through integrative motivation (indirect effect 0.28, 95% CI 0.20–0.36).
papers.takeaway: Suggests AI conversation practice can substantially boost speaking skills; groups were not randomized and the effect size is unusually large, so replication matters.

papers.title: Short-Form Video Exposure and Academic Strain: A Dose-Response Analysis and Acquiescence Diagnosis
papers.authors: Md. Alamgir Hossain
papers.summary: Among 863 students, short-form video addiction had the strongest link to academic strain (η² = 0.117), but a general 'agree with everything' response tendency drove much of the survey data and even flipped one result's sign.
findings: Survey of 863 university students using a 67-item battery covering seven constructs.
Short-form content addiction showed the strongest effect (η² = 0.117, ρ = 0.273, p < 0.001).
A general agreement factor explained 59–89% of construct variance; controlling for it turned the addiction–deep-learning link from +0.55 to −0.49.
papers.takeaway: Shows heavy short-video use tracks with academic strain, and that uncorrected survey response bias can reverse conclusions; cross-sectional self-report cannot establish cause.

papers.title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
papers.authors: Huiming Sun, Yue Li, Kangning Yang
papers.summary: A small purpose-trained judge found UI faults on screens better than the best frontier model (F1 0.48 vs 0.37) at about a hundredth of the cost.
findings: The small ProofJudge model reached F1 0.48 at locating UI faults, vs 0.37 for the strongest frontier judge (Gemini 4 Argon).
False alarms stayed within 15% on clean pages: 2% on real screenshots and 9% on generated pages.
Cost was roughly 1/100th of the frontier judge.
papers.takeaway: Cheap, specialized checkers can catch broken screens without a reference design; an F1 of 0.48 still means many faults are missed or mislocated.
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark vs frontier LLM judges

papers.title: Keeping LLM Agents on Procedure: Executable Finite-State Control for Long-Horizon Instruction Fidelity
papers.authors: Yutao Sun, Haokun Li, Mingshuai Chen
papers.summary: Wrapping an agent in an executable finite-state machine nearly tripled correct decisions on a 200-account procedure benchmark: Claude Haiku 4.5 got 139 right vs 48 for the best baseline.
findings: On a 200-account SOP-Bench batch, Haiku 4.5 with FSM control decided 139 accounts correctly vs 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of difference 46–130).
The FSM-guided Haiku ran at 38% of the cost of Claude Sonnet 4.6.
papers.takeaway: Hard-coding procedure structure around a cheap model can beat bigger models on long, rule-bound workflows; results come from one benchmark batch.

papers.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
papers.authors: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith
papers.summary: Sycophancy mostly appears before preference training: supervised fine-tuning checkpoints already reach at least 92% of the sycophancy of preference-aligned models.
findings: SFT checkpoints reached ≥92% of preference-aligned models' sycophancy scores and ≥85% of final models' scores.
Preference alignment raised sycophancy in only 4 of 9 model–benchmark cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points.
papers.takeaway: Fixing sycophancy likely needs attention to fine-tuning data, not just RLHF; findings cover a limited set of models and benchmarks.

papers.title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Ryan Liu, David Lee, Icey Siyi Ai
papers.summary: LLMs ace textbook questions about time (92.0–97.5%) yet underestimate how long their own tasks take by up to 99.5%, and some ignore a 1,200-fold jump in wait time.
findings: Models scored 92.0–97.5% on time-related theorem questions.
They underestimated their own completion times by as much as 99.5%.
Some LLMs did not adjust answers when a user's wait time grew 1,200-fold.
papers.takeaway: Knowing about time is not the same as reasoning with it, which matters for agents that plan or schedule; exact gaps vary by model.

papers.title: Adversarial Evaluation of Large Language Models for Patient-Friendly Radiology Report Summarization
papers.authors: Magdalini Paschali, Asad Aali, Arogya Koirala
papers.summary: When medical terms in radiology reports were swapped, LLMs hallucinated in roughly 28–42% of patient-friendly summaries, from GPT-5-mini (28.1–30.1%) to MedGemma (41.4–41.9%).
findings: 18,000 evaluation pairs across six LLMs.
Hallucination rates under term substitution: 28.1–30.1% GPT-5-mini, 35.3–36.4% Claude Sonnet 4.5, 41.4–41.9% MedGemma.
An LLM judge agreed with radiologists at macro-F1 0.55–0.56, close to radiologist–radiologist agreement of 0.53.
papers.takeaway: Patient-facing report summaries remain error-prone under realistic perturbations, and a domain-tuned model fared worst; this is an adversarial test, not routine clinical use.

papers.title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
papers.authors: Renee Jia, Di Mu, Yao Yu
papers.summary: An LLM-agent paper-trading account returned 34.5% from March 11 to August 28, 2026, more than double SPY's 14.4%, but with a deeper maximum drawdown.
findings: Paper-trading return of 34.5% vs 14.4% for SPY over the same dates (March 11–August 28, 2026).
Maximum drawdown was larger than the benchmark's.
papers.takeaway: Shows LLM agents can run a live trading loop, but one account over under six months, with more risk, is far from proof of a durable edge.

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning for an Options Market Maker: An Empirical Study with Real S&P 500 Options
papers.authors: Jacky Chen, Ing-Haw Cheng, John Hull
papers.summary: A risk-sensitive RL market maker cut tail losses 3.1% vs delta hedging on real S&P 500 options out of sample, and 8.9% in volatile falling markets, though it cost 7–10% in rising markets.
findings: Trained on 1996–2017 S&P 500 options data and tested out of sample on 2018–2023 with a TD3 agent.
CVaR tail loss was 3.1% lower than delta hedging overall, and 8.9% lower in volatile, falling markets.
The advantage reversed into a 7–10% cost in rising markets.
papers.takeaway: RL hedging helps most when markets crash, the moment that matters, but its edge is regime-dependent and modest overall.
papers.evidence: Preprint · out-of-sample backtest, 6 years of real options data

papers.title: The Effect of the U.S. Federal Production Tax Credit on Negative Energy Prices
papers.authors: Erik P. Johnson, Daniel H. Karney
papers.summary: Each 1% rise in wind output eligible for the federal production tax credit raises the chance of a negative wholesale power price by 3.4 percentage points on average.
findings: Causal analysis of Eastern Interconnection wholesale electricity markets, 2000–2023.
A 1% increase in PTC-eligible wind generation raised the probability of a negative price by 3.4 percentage points.
At least 18% of negative-price hours cannot be blamed on the PTC alone, and the credit explains about 10% of those it could explain.
papers.takeaway: Subsidy design measurably distorts power prices, but the PTC is only one of several drivers of negative pricing.
papers.evidence: Observational causal estimate · U.S. power markets 2000–2023
